source.name: Recovered headline sample
source.scopeNote: Fixed window 2019-02-06 through 2019-02-23 inclusive. The recovered set contains 9 dated headline records across three desks: four Guardian publisher-page items and five Mail/MailOnline titles transcribed in the 2020 High Court judgment, all dated 10 February. The court-listed titles are evidence of challenged items, not independent publisher page recoveries. This clustered, selected sample is insufficient to judge daily growth or compare overall coverage volume; missing records/dates are unknown, not zero.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would say readers had an interest in a public figure’s family dispute and in the father’s response to an earlier account. The court record lists two print headlines from 10 February. These are transcriptions from a later judgment, not recovered publisher pages or a census of our output.

One headline called the correspondence a “tragedy” and foregrounded a rift; the other paired a plea with the father’s response. We could argue that competing accounts served the public. But status alone does not make private correspondence public, especially when less intrusive reporting could explain the dispute.

At publication, the publisher argued the letter corrected inaccuracies and readers deserved the father’s reply. Those were contested claims. Later, the High Court and Court of Appeal found the five specified articles unlawful on privacy grounds; most disclosures were not a proportionate correction. A defence must acknowledge that result.

Our two titles share one date; they are not two separate events, and their original pages remain unrecovered. They show wording identified by the court, not total output or a daily trend. A responsible account would avoid repeating the letter, state the dispute’s status, and admit where the public-interest case fails.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend telling readers about the letter dispute and the father’s response, with the earlier People account as context. The court record lists three online headlines from 10 February. We have not recovered those original pages: these exact titles come from a later judgment and do not represent all our output.

Two titles repeat a broken-heart phrase; one uses a handwriting-based character label. We could argue that readers wanted the father’s reply and context. Yet a public figure’s status does not make private family correspondence public property. The character label risks judging personality instead of clarifying the dispute.

The publisher argued at the time that reporting corrected inaccuracies and gave the father a response. These were contested claims, not findings. The later High Court and Court of Appeal found the five challenged pieces unlawful on privacy grounds and the disclosures mostly disproportionate. That result weakens a correction-only defence.

Our three titles share one date and are listed in the court record; they do not establish daily growth, total site coverage, or separate underlying events. A responsible defence would explain purpose without reproducing the letter, distinguish claims from rulings, and admit the difficulty of defending the most personal framing.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: We would defend the 23 February report as coverage of a legal threat, not a court ruling. On 13 February, we also reported George Clooney’s criticism of press pursuit and publication of a daughter’s letter. Both items addressed public debate about reporting and legal rights, not the family dispute itself.

Our 16 February comment criticized the release of letter extracts; the 20 February column examined how both ordinary and grand gestures drew judgment. We would say scrutiny of that pattern served readers. Commentary still needs evidence and care: a person should not become a symbol or an invitation to judge her character.

Four recovered items span three dates, but this selection cannot show how often we covered Meghan. We would distinguish news from opinion and avoid counting each item as a separate event. The five challenged titles documented by the court belong to another publisher and are not a complete media count.

Later courts found five specific articles unlawful on privacy grounds; that does not decide every report or column. Our defence is that scrutiny of press conduct and a legal threat mattered publicly. It weakens wherever our wording amplified distress or invited judgment of the woman instead of the reporting.

publicContext.intro: Coverage in February 2019 centred on Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, her relationship with her father and publication of a private letter. Public curiosity and public interest are different questions. Later court findings about privacy and copyright provide context, while remaining separate from what editors knew at publication.
publicContext.allegationResponse: No private letter is reproduced here. A small recovered sample cannot establish the full scale of coverage or a matched comparison.

sequence.text: People published an article quoting friends and referencing a private letter to Thomas Markle.
The Mail on Sunday and MailOnline published extracts from the handwritten letter.
Reports described potential legal action and Thomas Markle’s response.
A Guardian-carried agency report published George Clooney’s criticism of the press pursuit and the publication of a daughter’s letter to her father.
Guardian comment discussed press treatment after extracts from the letter had been published.
Guardian comment criticized the scrutiny and vilification directed at Meghan.
